lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 3 you met pushes and pulls. What can a push do to a still ball? Make it start to move.
Energy is what makes things move, light up, warm up or make a sound. Anything that moves has energy of motion: a rolling ball, a horse galloping across a field, the wind turning a windmill's sails.
The faster something moves, the more energy of motion it has. A cart rolling slowly down a hill has a little energy. The same cart racing fast has much more.
How can we tell? Roll a ball slowly at a tower of blocks, then roll the same ball fast. The fast ball knocks more blocks down, and further: it had more energy to give.

When things bump into each other, it is called a collision. Energy moves from one thing to the other: when a rolling ball hits a still one, the first ball slows down and the second one starts to move.

Some of the energy in a collision turns into sound and a little heat. That is why a crash goes bang, and why your hands warm up when you rub them together. The energy is not lost: it moves on or changes.
Scientists ask questions and test them. Does a faster ball push a block further? Change only the speed, keep everything else the same, and measure how far the block goes.
In your worlds, a speed pad gives you a burst of speed. Faster means more energy of motion! Next: energy on the move.

exercises.prompt: Two balls are exactly alike. One rolls fast and one rolls slowly. Which has more energy?
exercises.hint: More speed, more energy.
exercises.explain: The faster ball has more energy of motion.

exercises.prompt: A ball that is not moving has no energy of motion.
exercises.hint: Energy of motion comes from moving.
exercises.explain: Only moving things have energy of motion. A still ball has none until something sets it rolling.

exercises.prompt: Which of these has energy of motion?
exercises.hint: Which one is moving?
exercises.explain: The rolling ball is moving, so it has energy of motion.

exercises.prompt: A cart rolling fast has more energy than the same cart rolling slowly.
exercises.hint: Which one is moving faster?
exercises.explain: The faster the cart, the more energy of motion it has.

exercises.prompt: Tilly rolls a ball slowly at a tower of blocks. Then she rolls the same ball fast. Which roll knocks more blocks down?
exercises.hint: Which roll gives the ball more energy?
exercises.explain: The fast ball has more energy to give to the blocks, so more of them fall.

exercises.prompt: A rolling ball hits a ball that is standing still. What happens?
exercises.hint: In a collision, energy moves from one thing to the other.
exercises.explain: Energy passes from the rolling ball to the still one: the still ball starts to move, and the first one slows down.
choices: The still ball starts to move

exercises.prompt: When two things bump into each other, some energy can turn into sound.
exercises.hint: What do you hear when things crash?
exercises.explain: That is the bang or the thud you hear in a collision.

exercises.prompt: Why do your hands get warm when you rub them together?
exercises.hint: Rubbing is motion. What can motion turn into?
exercises.explain: Rubbing turns some of the energy of motion into heat.
choices: Energy of motion turns into heat

exercises.prompt: It is the same buddy each time. Put these in order from least energy to most.
exercises.hint: The faster it moves, the more energy of motion it has.
exercises.explain: Standing still: no energy of motion. Walking: some. Running: the most.

exercises.prompt: Two identical carts crash into a wall. One was rolling fast, one slowly. Which crash is louder?
exercises.hint: Which cart has more energy that can change into sound?
exercises.explain: The fast cart had more energy, so more of it changed into sound: a louder crash.

exercises.prompt: A bowling ball rolls into the pins. Where does its energy go?
exercises.hint: Energy is never used up: it moves on or changes.
exercises.explain: The pins fly, you hear a crash, and a little heat is made: the energy moved on and changed.
choices: into moving pins, sound and a little heat
It all stays in the ball

exercises.prompt: In a collision, energy simply disappears.
exercises.hint: Think about where the energy goes.
exercises.explain: Energy never just disappears. It moves to the other thing, or changes into sound and heat.

exercises.prompt: Nell wants her marble to push a block further. What should she change?
exercises.hint: What gives the marble more energy?
exercises.explain: A faster marble has more energy, so it can push the block further.

exercises.prompt: Which question could you test to learn about energy in collisions?
exercises.hint: A test question can be answered by trying something and measuring it.
exercises.explain: You can roll a ball at different speeds and measure how far the block goes. The others cannot be tested that way.
choices: Does a faster ball push a block further?
Which colour of ball is the prettiest?
Who made the very first ball?

exercises.prompt: A ball rolls down a ramp and hits a block. Put what happens in order.
exercises.hint: Follow the energy from the ball to the block.
exercises.explain: The ball speeds up down the ramp, hits the block and passes on its energy; the block slides, then slows down and stops.
items: The block slows down and stops.
The block slides along the floor.
The ball speeds up as it rolls down.

exercises.prompt: Mimi drops the same ball twice: once from low down, once from high up. Which drop hits the ground harder?
exercises.hint: Which ball is moving faster when it reaches the ground?
exercises.explain: A ball falling from higher up is moving faster when it lands, so it has more energy and hits harder.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: has energy of motion, or not?
exercises.hint: Is it moving right now?
exercises.explain: Moving things have energy of motion: the galloping horse, the turning sails and the rolling ball. The parked cart and the book are still, so they have none.

exercises.prompt: Match each bump or rub to where some of its energy goes.
items: a ball hits a still ball
exercises.hint: Listen, feel and watch: what do you notice after each one?
exercises.explain: A bang is energy turned into sound. Rubbing hands turns it into heat. A ball hitting a still ball passes its energy on, so the other ball moves.

exercises.prompt: Nell tests: does a faster ball push a block further? Sort what she changes, keeps the same and measures.
exercises.hint: Only one thing may change, and you measure what it does.
exercises.explain: She changes only the ball's speed. She keeps the same ball, block and floor, and she measures how far the block slides. Then the speed is the only cause of any difference.

exercises.prompt: The same cart each time: order these from the least energy of motion to the most.
items: a cart racing down a steep hill
a cart parked at the top
a cart rolling slowly down a gentle hill
exercises.hint: Which cart is still, which is slow, and which is fast?
exercises.explain: Parked at the top: no energy of motion. Rolling slowly: a little. Racing down a steep hill: the most, because it moves fastest.
